output:
*Interview with Rosa Häfeli, maid and cook, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Sit down, Mademoiselle Häfeli. You are very pale. Take your time.

ROSA: Herrgott, I cannot sit. I keep thinking I must go back and see to the glasses.

MATTHEY: Tell me about the evening, from the beginning, as much as you are able.

ROSA: There was the goose, and the soup before it. Madame wanted everything exact, as always. I had washed the champagne glasses for the toast and put them on the tray, and I had the bottle cooling in the cellar. Then it was all for the dining room, and I was in the kitchen.

MATTHEY: You stayed in the kitchen for the whole evening?

ROSA: Where else would I be, Monsieur? Madame does not want the maid in the dining room with the gentlemen.

MATTHEY: I see there is a clock in the kitchen.

ROSA: The American one, on the shelf over the stove. It is a quarter of an hour fast. I keep it so on purpose, so nothing is ever late. The soup is never late, the bread is never late, and Madame is never kept waiting for her dinner. Monsieur Monnier laughed at me for it, but he never said I was wrong.

MATTHEY: Are you certain of the quarter hour?

ROSA: I am certain, Monsieur. I have checked it against the temple many times.

MATTHEY: Did anyone come down to the kitchen during the evening?

ROSA: Fräulein Lina came down into the kitchen at thirteen minutes to eleven by my kitchen clock, and she stayed with me until after the temple struck eleven. She sat by the stove. I put the kettle on for her and she did not drink it. She does not talk much, that one. She is careful with her hands, the way the master taught her.

MATTHEY: While you were together, did you hear anything from the rest of the house?

ROSA: Madame's piano. We heard it begin at two minutes to eleven by my kitchen clock. It was Chopin, as it always is when there are guests. It stopped at eleven minutes past eleven by my kitchen clock. Madame plays very well, Monsieur, better than anyone who comes to the house.

MATTHEY: You are sure of those two times?

ROSA: I am sure of what my clock showed. I cannot tell you better than the clock.

MATTHEY: Did you hear the hall clock?

ROSA: I heard the hall clock strike eleven when my kitchen clock showed thirteen minutes past eleven. I did not think about it then. Why would I?

MATTHEY: Later you went up to the atelier.

ROSA: I went up to fetch Monsieur for the toast. Madame had said the glasses were ready and he must come down. I thought he had forgotten, as he sometimes does when he is working. The door was open and I saw him on the floor by his bench. There was blood on the boards. I did not touch him. I could see he was dead, Monsieur, I did not need to touch him. He had his watch in his hand, the little one he had been making for four years.

MATTHEY: Did you go into any other room on the way?

ROSA: I went up the stairs and I came down them. I did not stop anywhere. I did not know what to do with my hands.

MATTHEY: Nothing in that is a fault. You will not be blamed for what you found.

ROSA: Am I to be taken away? I have never been in a police room. My mother would not believe it.

MATTHEY: You are not under arrest. I want only what you saw and heard in your kitchen and on the stairs.

ROSA: Madame has been good to me. She will not cry in front of you, Monsieur, so do not expect it. She is not a woman who weeps. If you need anything from her, you must ask her plainly, the way she likes to be asked.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Mademoiselle Häfeli. Please wait in the hall. We may need you again.

ROSA: Ja. I will wait. Herrgott, the glasses are still on the tray.
